section_summary: This section documents U.S. and British efforts in early 1941 to monitor and restrict supplies of strategic materials—especially petroleum, aviation gasoline, metals, and scrap—to Japan and, indirectly, Germany and Italy. A large British dossier analyzes Japanese and Thai oil imports, reserves, storage, tanker capacity, and possible controls, while diplomatic reporting traces suspicious cobalt and tungsten shipments from Bolivia and measures against scrap exports in the Dominican Republic and Costa Rica. The section also contains congressional and commercial inquiries about U.S. export licensing and several cross-reference sheets concerning Japanese procurement.

subfiles.title: Strategic Materials in the American Republics and Abnormal Shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: W. Y. Elliott, Office of Production Management
subfiles.to: Dean G. Acheson, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Recommends U.S. purchasing and licensing measures to prevent Latin American strategic materials from reaching Japan, Germany, and Italy.
subfiles.summary: Elliott's concluding section covers buying strategic metals in Peru, Chile, Colombia and Argentina, with appendices on Latin American commodities and abnormal Japanese purchases; he urges buying entire outputs and licensing exports.

subfiles.title: Supplemental Note on Toluol at Tampico
subfiles.about: Reports a ship at Tampico believed to hold 2,600 tons of toluol and asks whether Mexico could acquire it for U.S. strategic reserves.
subfiles.summary: Elliott relays Dr. Morgan's concern that a toluol shortage makes the Tampico cargo valuable, its price well above U.S. levels, leaving action to State.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Elliott's Strategic-Materials Letters
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Elliott's two March 6 letters concerning strategic-material shipments from other American republics to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Acheson thanks Elliott, saying the Department knows many of the situations and is acting or considering action.

subfiles.title: Confidential Instruction to the Embassy in Mexico Regarding Tampico Toluol
subfiles.about: Transmits Elliott's report of a Tampico toluol stock and requests the Embassy's confidential comment.
subfiles.summary: Confidential instruction to the Mexico Embassy, enclosing Elliott's March 6 letter, asks it to assess the reported 2,600-ton Tampico toluol cargo and possible Mexican action.

subfiles.title: Copy of Elliott's March 6 Toluol Letter
subfiles.about: Provides the enclosure copy of Elliott's warning about the toluol cargo at Tampico.
subfiles.summary: Copy of Elliott's March 6 letter: a ship may hold 2,600 tons of toluol that Dr. Morgan wanted Mexico to acquire.

subfiles.title: Conversation Between Secretary Hull and Lord Halifax on an Export Embargo
subfiles.from: Office of the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Records Lord Halifax's presentation of British papers on Japanese strategic purchases and gasoline exports.
subfiles.summary: Halifax raises a gasoline export embargo on Japan; Hull says it is under study and asks what parallel British action is possible, noting U.S. consideration of limits on lubricating oils and fats.

subfiles.title: British Memorandum on Preventing Japanese Strategic Stockpiling
subfiles.about: Urges a coordinated policy to prevent Japan from accumulating strategic reserves beyond current consumption needs.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that continued excessive imports weaken the democracies' economic leverage and make future Japanese aggression easier. It proposes export licensing, shipping restrictions, preemption in Latin America, and limits on imports from Japan, coordinated through a centralized U.S. interdepartmental unit. Oil is singled out for immediate expert examination.

subfiles.title: British Note on Urgent Oil Controls for Japan
subfiles.about: Requests agreement on limiting Japanese oil imports, especially through restrictions on non-Japanese tankers.
subfiles.summary: The note cites sharply increased Japanese purchases of aviation-grade gasoline and excessive stocks in Thailand. Britain proposes reducing annual Japanese imports by about 7.5 million barrels through coordinated tanker restrictions while relying on U.S. licensing to control dangerous grades. It asks for immediate discussion by a centralized American committee.

subfiles.title: Japanese Oil Situation
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan's dependence on imported petroleum and advocates joint restrictions on further stock accumulation.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum reviews Japan's oil sources, wartime needs and reserves, questions U.S. Navy consumption figures, and proposes denying Japan foreign-controlled tankers as less provocative than an overt embargo.

subfiles.title: Index to Statements Regarding Japan
subfiles.about: Lists the statistical statements and memoranda supporting the British oil-policy case.
subfiles.summary: Index to statements on Japanese petroleum imports, oil stocks, tanker capacity, aviation gasoline, the Batavia agreement and the Anglo-Iranian contract, for the following annexes.

subfiles.title: Japanese Empire Imports of All Petroleum Products, 1937–1940
subfiles.about: Tabulates Japanese petroleum imports by source and explains shipments from secondary suppliers.
subfiles.summary: The tables compare imports from the United States, Netherlands East Indies, Malaya, Borneo, Sakhalin, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Mexico, Peru, Ecuador, Russia, and Romania. Notes explain company control, crude-oil contracts, and the composition of shipments, including Peruvian and Ecuadorian exports. Revised figures add estimated 1940 totals.

subfiles.title: U.S. Exports of Petroleum Products to Japan
subfiles.about: Lists annual U.S. petroleum-product exports to Japan and its included territories from 1937 through 1940.
subfiles.summary: Table of U.S. petroleum product exports to Japan, including Korea, Taiwan and Pacific island territories but excluding Manchuria and Kwantung.

subfiles.title: U.S. Exports of Petroleum Products to Kwantung
subfiles.about: Reports U.S. petroleum exports to Kwantung, including Port Arthur and Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Annual table of U.S. petroleum product exports to Kwantung, much presumably for Manchuria.

subfiles.title: November–December 1940 U.S. Petroleum Exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Compares petroleum exports to Japan in November and December 1940 with the 1939 monthly average.
subfiles.summary: Table of large November-December 1940 U.S. petroleum exports to Japan, supporting the British view that imports stayed high after the Batavia agreement.

subfiles.title: Oil Stocks—Japan
subfiles.about: Estimates Japanese oil stocks by reconciling imports, domestic and synthetic production, and consumption during 1937–1939.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum adopts a working estimate of about 39.5 million barrels of Japanese oil stocks at end-1939; British estimates suggest the Navy overstated Army consumption, so actual stocks could be higher.

subfiles.title: Japan—Oil Storage Capacity
subfiles.about: Estimates commercial and government petroleum-storage capacity in Japan and lists recent steel-tank shipments.
subfiles.summary: Known storage is placed at approximately 43.7 million barrels, divided among Standard Vacuum, Shell, Japanese companies, naval storage, and the Kyodo Kigyo government company. The statement then lists tanks shipped from American West Coast ports aboard several Japanese vessels, totaling about 3.5 million barrels of prospective additional capacity.

subfiles.title: Carrying Capacity of the Japanese Tanker Fleet
subfiles.about: Calculates how much petroleum Japan could import using its own tankers, whalers, and naval auxiliaries.
subfiles.summary: Japan's tanker fleet carries about 425,000 tons, allowing annual imports of roughly 30 to 35.85 million barrels in Japanese vessels.

subfiles.title: Shipments of Aviation Gasoline to Japan
subfiles.about: Lists tanker and packaged shipments of aviation-quality gasoline from U.S. ports to Japan during August–December 1940.
subfiles.summary: Schedule of aviation-gasoline shipments to Japan totaling nearly one million barrels, below the formal threshold but able to reach aviation quality with tetraethyl lead.

subfiles.title: Summary of the Batavia Oil Agreement
subfiles.about: Summarizes the November 1940 agreement between Royal Dutch Shell and Standard Oil interests and Japanese importers.
subfiles.summary: Summary of the Batavia agreement: about 1.8 million tons of petroleum yearly from the Netherlands East Indies, with company shares and Japanese quotas, far below Japan's original demands.

subfiles.title: Anglo-Iranian Japanese Contract
subfiles.about: Describes an Anglo-Iranian Oil Company contract to sell Iranian crude oil to Japanese buyers.
subfiles.summary: Anglo-Iranian contract: twelve cargoes from Abadan, only three delivered by January 1941; the company rejected Japanese substitution of gasoline or diesel, and the Shah's royalty pressure played a part.

subfiles.title: British Memorandum on Oil Supplies to Thailand
subfiles.about: Urges controls preventing Thailand from accumulating oil stocks that could become available to Japan.
subfiles.summary: British memorandum fears excessive Thai stocks of 86-octane gasoline usable against Burma, Malaya or the East Indies and proposes regular limits rather than an embargo.

subfiles.title: Thai Oil Stocks and Recent and Impending Shipments
subfiles.about: Estimates Thai petroleum stocks and adds known U.S. shipments received after December 1, 1940.
subfiles.summary: Annex estimating Thai oil stocks in months of supply, listing shipments by tanker and projecting early-March stocks; aviation fuel stocks seemed enough for two to three years.

subfiles.title: Thai Ministry of Defence Six-Month Fuel Requirements
subfiles.from: Fuel Department, Thai Ministry of Defence
subfiles.about: States claimed six-month Thai requirements for aviation gasoline, motor spirit, diesel, gas oil, bunker fuel, and kerosene.
subfiles.summary: Thai Ministry of Defence six-month fuel requirements total over two million barrels, judged far above normal needs.

subfiles.title: U.S. Exports of Petroleum Products to Thailand
subfiles.about: Tabulates U.S. petroleum exports to Thailand from 1937 through 1940.
subfiles.summary: Table of U.S. petroleum product exports to Thailand; Netherlands East Indies companies withdrew from Thai marketing in July 1939.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 299 on Dominican Scrap-Iron Export Controls
subfiles.about: Reports that the Dominican government prohibited export of scrap iron after concern about 1,000 tons allegedly assembled for shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The despatch refers to presidential assurances that the scrap would not be shipped to Japan. It encloses a customs circular forbidding scrap-iron exports without special authorization and attributes the action directly to the Legation's conversation with President Troncoso.

subfiles.title: Dominican Customs Circular No. 463
subfiles.about: Orders customs offices not to permit exports of scrap iron without prior authorization.
subfiles.summary: Dominican Customs Circular 463 orders all customs offices to enforce the prohibition starting February 25, 1941.

subfiles.title: Translation of Dominican Customs Circular No. 463
subfiles.about: Provides the English translation of the Dominican order prohibiting unauthorized scrap-iron exports.
subfiles.summary: Translation of the circular: scrap iron needs prior Treasury and Commerce authorization, and all customs offices must comply.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2964 on Used Rails in Costa Rica
subfiles.from: William H. Hornibrook, American Legation, San José
subfiles.about: Reports the local sale of discarded Pacific Railway rails after Japanese purchasers had been excluded.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 2964: the Pacific Railway sold rails to a local company and 8,000 to Solera & Company to buy diesel locomotives; the aim of rewarding Costa Rica's refusal to sell to Japan was met, and remaining rails could go to American buyers.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Japanese Motor-Fuel Problems
subfiles.about: Points to a Batavia despatch enclosing a Netherlands consul general's report on Japanese motor-fuel problems.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Kobe report of November 10, 1940 on Japanese motor-fuel problems, with translation, filed at 894.6363/367.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Correspondence Concerning Exports to Japan
subfiles.about: References a congressional letter enclosing correspondence from F. C. Fisher about exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference on correspondence about exports to Japan, directing to file 862.24/351.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Greek Merchant Vessels Carrying Scrap Iron at Honolulu
subfiles.about: References a Navy Department report on nine Greek merchant ships at Honolulu carrying scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Greek merchant vessels carrying scrap iron at Honolulu, filed at 868.8591/24.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Argentine Tungsten Exports to Japan
subfiles.about: References a telegram reporting that 125.3 tons of tungsten ore went to Japan in November and December 1940.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Argentine tungsten shipment to Japan, about 40 percent of exports, in telegram 116 of the defense-materials file.

subfiles.title: Kirwan Transmittal of Constituent Correspondence
subfiles.doc_type: congressional covering letter and routing sheet
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's letter for investigation and information needed to prepare a reply.
subfiles.summary: Kirwan asks the Department to investigate the enclosed statements and return the correspondence with an answer. The following page records departmental filing and routing information.

subfiles.title: W. L. Countryman Letter on Military Service and War-Supply Exports
subfiles.about: Requests selective-service legislation and asks whether the United States still permits war-useful exports to Japan and Russia.
subfiles.summary: W. L. Countryman asks for the act authorizing training of men aged 21 to 36, and objects to motor fuel, scrap, and copper exports to Japan and Russia as undermining confidence in war policy. Page 112 duplicates it.

subfiles.title: State Department Reply to Michael J. Kirwan
subfiles.about: Explains statutory export-control authority and licensing policy in response to Countryman's concerns.
subfiles.summary: State cites section 6 of the July 2, 1940 act: aviation gasoline and scrap iron go only to the British Empire and Western Hemisphere, other licenses are sparing, and none issues if defense may be endangered.

subfiles.title: British Embassy Letter on the Toei Maru Aviation-Petrol Shipment
subfiles.about: Transmits intelligence about a large aviation-petrol shipment from San Francisco to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Butler encloses a San Francisco telegram and Hill's comment: the Toei Maru sailed February 22 for Japan with about 80,000 barrels of aviation-base petrol for Mitsubishi in dirty tanks.

subfiles.title: Telegram and Comment on Accelerated Japanese Aviation-Petrol Shipments
subfiles.about: Reports intelligence that Japan was accelerating shipments in anticipation of a possible March crisis.
subfiles.summary: Telegram on loading 71-72-octane aviation petrol into the uncleaned Toei Maru amid rising freight rates; Hill says it may be 86-octane, several years of Australian needs.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of British Aviation-Gasoline Information
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Butler's letter and enclosure concerning Pacific Coast aviation-gasoline shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Butler for the material. The short reply formally records receipt of the British intelligence.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 695 on Cobalt Ore from Bolivia to Japan
subfiles.about: Investigates a concealed shipment of approximately 29 tons of Bolivian cobalt ore apparently intended for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 695: Bolivian cobalt ore from the Liones mine, ostensibly for New York, returned to Valparaiso and Antofagasta awaiting a Japanese ship; bags were to be remarked for Mitsui with origin and destination hidden, so the Legation urges a New York investigation.

subfiles.title: Overseas Metal & Ore Corporation Instructions for the Cobalt Consignment
subfiles.to: Caja de Crédito Minero de Antofagasta
subfiles.about: Orders the removal of Bolivian marks, re-marking for Osaka, controlled sampling, and secret delivery of cobalt ore to Mitsui.
subfiles.summary: Overseas Metal & Ore letter on 1,210 bags of cobalt: make Banco Minero marks invisible, mark for Osaka, release to Mitsui after payment, and keep origin and buyer secret from each other.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Bolivian Cobalt Despatch to Export Control
subfiles.about: Forwards the La Paz despatch and its enclosure regarding cobalt ore carried on the Chilean vessel Imperial.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum sends Export Control the Bolivian cobalt despatch and concealment instructions, answering the Division's February 17 request.

subfiles.title: Finletter Transmittal to Mr. Clayton
subfiles.about: Confidentially transmits a copy of the March 10 La Paz despatch about cobalt ore shipped from Bolivia to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Finletter sends Mr. Clayton the Bolivian cobalt report for confidential information.

subfiles.title: Finletter Transmittal to Mr. Masters
subfiles.about: Confidentially transmits the La Paz report on the Bolivian cobalt shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Finletter's second distribution letter, to Mr. Masters, on the same March 10 despatch.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 696 on Alleged Bolivian Tungsten Shipments to Japan
subfiles.doc_type: confidential diplomatic despatch with duplicate copies
subfiles.from: Douglas Jenkins, American Legation, La Paz
subfiles.about: Reports allegations that Bolivian tungsten nominally consigned to the United States was ultimately reaching Japan and possibly Germany.
subfiles.summary: Two sources, including one in Bolivian mining circles, reported that tungsten shipments traveled north in double bags. The outer bags bore markings matching the ostensible U.S. consignment, while inner bags could show or later receive the true destination. Pages 129–131 reproduce additional file copies of the same despatch.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Bolivian Tungsten Despatch
subfiles.from: Leonard H. Price, Assistant Chief, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Forwards the March 10 La Paz despatch on alleged Bolivian tungsten shipments to Japan through the United States.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum circulates a copy of the diplomatic report for information. It identifies the enclosure by origin, number, and date.

subfiles.title: Inquiry About Exporting Terne-Plate Scrap
subfiles.from: Meyer Lipkin, Franklin Waste & Metal Company
subfiles.about: Asks whether terne-plate scrap may be exported to Japan or another Asian country when no domestic market exists.
subfiles.summary: Lipkin asks whether terne-plate scrap, with no domestic use and harmful in steel melts, falls under the banned-export list.

subfiles.title: State Department Reply on Terne-Plate Scrap Exports
subfiles.from: Hallett Johnson, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that terne-plate scrap may be exported only under license and describes the government's destination policy.
subfiles.summary: The reply cites regulations issued under the President's December 10, 1940 proclamation. Iron and steel exports outside the Western Hemisphere and British Empire were permitted only in accordance with customary prewar shipments. Johnson apologizes for the delayed response caused by the volume of export applications.
